title: Justice Tarot Card Meaning: Upright, Reversed & Love
description: Justice upright: fairness, truth; reversed: imbalance, avoiding your part. Love, work, advice, Waite's 1911 text and the 1909 card. Ask your question.
image_alt: Justice, 1909 Rider–Waite–Smith card: a crowned figure in a red robe and green cape sits between two grey pillars before a purple curtain, holding an upright sword and a pair of scales.
capsule: Justice is card XI of the Major Arcana: fairness, truth, cause and effect, and owning your choices. Reversed, it points to unfairness, dishonesty or avoiding your part. It is a fair card rather than a harsh one, and what it asks for is honesty. Yes or no is not clear yet: the scales are still weighing.

blocks.heading: What is on the Justice card?
paragraphs: A crowned figure sits between two grey stone pillars with a purple curtain hung behind her. In her right hand she holds a sword straight up; from her left hangs a pair of scales. Waite keeps his comments short, because the card "follows the traditional symbolism and carries above all its obvious meanings" (p. 112).

The sword is what stands out most, its blue blade rising almost to the top edge. On the 1909 card her robe is red, a green cape is fastened at her throat, her crown has a square stone at the front, the strip of background above the curtain is yellow, and XI is printed at the top. The scales hang low at her side, and a white shoe shows beneath the hem.

Waite points out one detail on purpose: the figure is "seated between pillars, like the High Priestess" (p. 112). He ends with a contrast between the two cards: "the pillars of Justice open into one world and the pillars of the High Priestess into another" (p. 115).

blocks.heading: What did Waite write about Justice?
paragraphs: The upright list opens with everyday fairness words: equity, rightness, probity. Its last item and the first two of the reversed list speak the language of law; the rest of that list names faults of judgment: bigotry, bias, too much severity. On Arcana Diary, Justice is never read about legal matters or how they end; it is read only as honesty and balance in your own choices.

Waite also separates two ideas. One is the moral principle "which deals unto every man according to his works"; the other is a spiritual justice that, in his words, has no "canon of criticism or ground of explanation" (p. 112).

blocks.heading: What does Justice mean upright?
paragraphs: Upright, Justice asks for fairness and truth: seeing a situation as it really is, your own part included. It often turns up when a decision is in front of you and you want to make it cleanly.

Accountability sits at the heart of the card. That is not blame. It means owning your choices and their effects, the welcome ones and the awkward ones, so that you act in a way you would still stand behind later. Cause and effect belongs here too: choices carry their fair results, and the card is often read as an outcome that matches what was put in.

Balance is the other theme. Weigh the facts, not only your feelings about them, and ask whether an arrangement is fair to everyone it touches, you as well. A useful question here: what would the honest version of this choice look like? Modern readings also link the card to legal matters and contracts, meaning agreements read carefully and terms that are clear and fair.

blocks.heading: What does Justice mean reversed?
paragraphs: Reversed, Justice can point to imbalance: an arrangement that feels uneven, a sense of unfairness, dishonesty, or a habit of avoiding your part in what went wrong.

It can also turn inward as harsh self-judgment, holding yourself to a stricter standard than the facts support. That inward reading is a modern one, not Waite's; the nearest words on his reversed list are "excessive severity".
Either way, the repair starts with honest sorting: what is truly yours to answer for, and what is not. Take responsibility for the first and put the second down.

blocks.heading: What does Justice mean in love?
paragraphs: Give and take is what the scales weigh in love, and upright the card stands for a truthful, balanced bond in which both people carry their share. When you share a life with someone, the card invites an honest look at balance: who carries what, which needs get said out loud, which agreements still fit.
Single, you might ask whether what you hope for from a future partner matches what you are ready to offer, and whether your standards are fair to you as well.

With the scales upside down, the card is read as a one-sided or unfair bond, or a lack of honesty in love. Notice where things feel lopsided, or where you avoid looking at your share of a problem that keeps coming back. What would a fairer arrangement look like to you?

blocks.heading: What does Justice mean for work and money?
paragraphs: Clear agreements, honest feedback and decisions you can explain are Justice's ground at work. It can be a moment to review how tasks are split or a promise you made, and to check that it is fair to everyone involved.
Justice's money meaning is fair dealing: pay that matches the work, agreements kept on both sides, accounts that balance, and choices built on facts rather than on assumptions you have never checked.

If it comes up reversed, it can mean an unfair deal, money that is owed, or a lack of transparency about costs. Look for an arrangement that has slipped out of balance, or a mistake you would rather not name.

blocks.heading: What is Justice's advice?
paragraphs: Divide a page into two columns, facts and assumptions, and sort what you know about your situation. Then decide from the first column. Whatever lands in the second deserves a check before you act, or before you judge anyone, yourself included.

blocks.heading: Is Justice a yes or no card?
Justice as a person and as feelings
paragraphs: Justice tends to describe someone fair-minded who hears both sides and says what is true, even when it is uncomfortable. Turned toward you, it shows your wish to do the right thing and to own it. When the question is about feelings, the card stands for respect and serious intentions: considered affection that weighs things before it commits and wants the relationship to be fair to both people. Reversed, the feelings are out of balance: one side giving more than the other, resentment over something unfair, guilt bigger than the facts, or feelings that are not being stated honestly.

pairs.text: Fairness meets moderation. Look for the middle ground and give it time rather than forcing a quick decision.
An honest review that opens something new. Look at past choices clearly, then answer what is calling you now.
Balance in a bond between equals. Check whether the give and take still feels even to you.
Carrying more than your share. Sort out what is truly yours to hold and hand the rest back.

blocks.heading: Justice or the Two of Swords?
paragraphs: Both cards show a woman holding a blade and facing a question of balance. In the Two of Swords, Waite describes "a hoodwinked female figure" who "balances two swords upon her shoulders" (p. 250): her eyes are covered, and the balance holds only because nothing is decided. Justice looks straight ahead and weighs with open eyes before choosing. Putting off a choice points to the Two of Swords; facing it squarely points to Justice.

blocks.heading: Questions to ask yourself about Justice
paragraphs: Which part of this situation is mine to own, and which is not?
Am I deciding from facts or from assumptions?
Am I judging myself more harshly than the facts support?

faq.q: Is Justice a good or bad card?
faq.a: Neither, strictly speaking; it is an even-handed card. It rewards honesty and asks you to own what is yours, which can sting before it brings relief. The trouble it can point to is imbalance, or being too severe with others or with yourself. Fair does not mean harsh: the card asks for honesty, not punishment.

faq.q: Why is Justice card 11 and not 8?
faq.a: Because Waite moved it. He notes that Justice is "usually numbered eight" and that he swapped it with Strength "for reasons which satisfy myself", adding that the change "carries nothing with it which will signify to the reader" (p. 100). On the 1909 card, and on Arcana Diary, it is XI.

faq.q: Who is the woman on the Justice card?
faq.a: Waite gives her no name of his own. He reports that she "is said to be Astræa", a goddess who stood for the same virtue with the same symbols, then insists that the Tarot "is not of Roman mythology, or of Greek either" (pp. 21–22). For a reading, she is simply fairness given a human shape.

faq.q: Does Justice mean I am being judged?
faq.a: Not by the card. Justice invites you to look at a situation with fair eyes, and that includes looking at yourself without cruelty. If drawing it leaves you feeling accused, read its reversed side: severity beyond what happened is exactly what it cautions against.

waite.quote: Equity, rightness, probity, executive; triumph of the deserving side in law. Reversed: Law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity.
